Tis study presents the Zagreb Eta indices, a novel family of degree-based topological descriptors defned through multiplicative
combinations of neighboring vertex degrees, designed to model the physicochemical properties of benzenoid hydrocarbons.
Building on our prior work that proposed the additive Zagreb upsilon indices, we intentionally reused the same dataset of 24
benzenoid compounds—including boiling point, π-electron energy, molecular weight, polarizability, molar volume, and molar
refractivity—to directly compare predictive performance and structural sensitivity. We computed the frst, second, and third Eta
indices from hydrogen-suppressed molecular graphs and evaluated their correlations with physicochemical properties using
Pearson correlation coefcients and linear regression models. Additionally, smoothness analysis based on structural sensitivity
and abruptness metrics was conducted to assess model stability and discriminative power. Te Eta indices achieved exceptionally
high correlation coefcients, up to 0.9998 for π-electron energy and over 0.9995 for polarizability and molar refractivity.
Compared to classical indices and the previously introduced upsilon indices, the Eta indices demonstrated comparable or slightly
superior predictive capacity while maintaining desirable smoothness characteristics. Tese results suggest that the multiplicative
formulation of the Eta indices captures complementary structural information, underscoring their potential value as robust
descriptors in QSPR modeling and highlighting the importance of alternative topological approaches in cheminformatics.
Keywords: benzenoid derivatives; degree-based topological indices; Eta degree; QSPR analysis; Zagreb Eta indices
1. Introduction
Te use of topological indices as numerical descriptors of
molecular structures has become an indispensable tool in
quantitative structure–property relationship (QSPR) and
quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) mod-
eling. Since the pioneering works of Wiener [1], Platt [2],
and later Gutman and Trinajsti´c [3], thousands of distinct
topological indices have been introduced, each designed to
capture diferent aspects of molecular graphs such as size,
branching, cyclicity, and degree distributions [4, 5]. Tese
indices enable researchers to construct mathematical models
linking structural features of chemical compounds to ex-
perimentally
measured
physicochemical
or
biological
properties, facilitating predictions in drug discovery, ma-
terial design, and environmental chemistry.
Te family of Zagreb-type indices, which includes the
well-known frst and second Zagreb indices, has been par-
ticularly infuential due to their simplicity and strong cor-
relation with various molecular properties. Over the past
decades, numerous variants have been proposed, often dif-
fering in how they combine vertex degrees to represent
molecular branching and complexity. Such indices have been
widely used to predict boiling points (BPs), molecular weight
(MW), π-electron energy (Pi-ele), polarizability (PO), molar
refractivity (MR), and other key molecular descriptors. Similar
studies exploring degree-based topological descriptors and
their QSPR performance can be found in recent works [6–8].
In our previous study [7], we introduced a novel set of
degree-based indices termed the Zagreb upsilon indices, for-
mulated to capture additive contributions of vertex degrees in
benzenoid hydrocarbons. By analyzing a dataset of structurally

Te formulation of topological indices continues to
evolve, as researchers recognize that diferent mathematical
constructions can refect complementary aspects of mo-
lecular structure. In this context, the present study in-
troduces the Zagreb Eta indices—a distinct class of degree-
based descriptors derived from the Eta degree concept,
which defnes each vertex through the product of its
neighboring vertex degrees. Unlike the previously proposed
Zagreb upsilon indices that depend on additive relation-
ships, the Eta indices emphasize multiplicative degree in-
teractions, ofering a refned way to represent local
branching intensity and complex connectivity within mo-
lecular graphs.
Te motivation for introducing the Eta indices is
twofold. First, by changing the mathematical formulation
from summation to multiplication, we seek to test
whether the new indices provide stronger or comple-
mentary correlations with physicochemical properties.
Second, we aim to evaluate whether the Eta indices ofer
diferent
sensitivity
and
smoothness
character-
istics—qualities important for the stability and in-
terpretability of QSPR models.
To maintain consistency and ensure an equitable basis
for comparison, the present study deliberately reuses the
same dataset of benzenoid hydrocarbons examined in earlier
research. Tis controlled design enables a direct comparative
evaluation between the newly introduced Zagreb Eta indices,
the previously defned upsilon indices, and several classical
degree-based topological descriptors such as the Randi´c (R),
atom–bond connectivity (ABC), Augmented Zagreb (AZI),
and Sombor (SO) indices. Trough systematic computation
of
correlation
coefcients,
regression
modeling,
and
smoothness assessment via structural sensitivity (SS) and
abruptness (Abr) parameters, this work aims to compre-
hensively evaluate the modeling performance and in-
terpretability of the Zagreb Eta indices.
Furthermore, this study contributes theoretically by
discussing the mathematical properties and chemical in-
terpretability of the Eta indices, situating them within the
broader landscape of graph-theoretical molecular de-
scriptors. We argue that the multiplicative formulation may
capture aspects of molecular branching that additive indices
might overlook, particularly in aromatic systems charac-
terized by conjugation and planar structures.
Te remainder of this paper is organized as follows:
Section 2 defnes the Eta degree and the three forms of
Zagreb Eta indices; Section 3 details the dataset, its physi-
cochemical parameters, and computational procedures;
Section 4 provides correlation and regression analyses;
Section 5 discusses theoretical aspects and interpretative
implications; Section 6 investigates smoothness behavior;
and Section 7 addresses the limitations and future research
perspectives. Te conclusion summarizes the essential
outcomes and contributions of the study.
2. Materials and Methods
2.1.DatasetandRationaleforReuse. Te dataset employed in
this work comprises 24 benzenoid hydrocarbons, encom-
passing representative compounds such as benzene, naph-
thalene, phenanthrene, anthracene, and several higher
polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. Te same dataset, to-
gether with its physicochemical attributes—including BP,
Pi-ele, MW, PO, molar volume (MV), and MR—was pre-
viously compiled and utilized in our earlier publication that
introduced the Zagreb upsilon indices [7].
Te intentional reuse of this dataset in the present study
serves a scientifc purpose: it enables a controlled and fair
comparative analysis of the predictive performance and SS of
the newly proposed Zagreb Eta indices against both the pre-
viously introduced upsilon indices and several well-established
degree-based topological descriptors. Tis controlled compar-
ison helps isolate the efect of the index defnition itself, rather
than confounding results by changes in dataset composition.

originate from the notion of the Eta degree (η(v)) associated
with a vertex v in a connected graph G. Mathematically, the
Eta degree of a vertex is represented as the product of the
degrees of all its adjacent vertices:

2.3. Calculation of Indices and Comparative Descriptors.
For each compound in the dataset, the frst, second, and third
variants of the Zagreb Eta indices were computed using the
hydrogen-suppressed molecular graph of the corresponding
structure. In parallel, several well-established degree-based
topological descriptors—including the frst and second
Zagreb indices (M1 and M2), R, ABC, AZI, Geometric–
arithmetic (GA), and SO indices—were also calculated to
enable a comparative evaluation of their performance.
Te chemical structures were drawn using ChemDraw
Ultra 12.0, and graph-theoretical computations were carried
out using custom scripts developed in Python, following
standard algorithms described in the literature [5].

2.4. Statistical Analysis. To examine the predictive strength
of the proposed Zagreb Eta indices, Pearson correlation
coefcients (R) were determined between each index and the
six physicochemical parameters included in the dataset. In
addition, simple linear regression models were established to
evaluate the degree and direction of association between the
indices and the selected molecular properties.
A smoothness investigation was also carried out by
estimating SS and Abr values for the Eta indices. Te
procedure followed the approach introduced by Furtula et al.
[5] and was applied to tree graphs consisting of four to nine
vertices. Tis enabled a comparative assessment of the
smoothness tendencies of the Zagreb Eta indices relative to
well-known degree-based descriptors.
All statistical analyses and plots were performed using
standard Python libraries (numPy, pandas, sciPy, and
matplotlib).
Te exploration of topological indices dates back to 1947,
when Harold Wiener proposed the frst distance-based
descriptor to predict the BPs of alkanes [1]. Te Wiener
index, based on the sum of pairwise vertex distances in
a molecular graph, became a cornerstone in the development
of chemical graph theory. Interestingly, the Zagreb index
was not the earliest degree-based index; this distinction
belongs to the Platt index, which was also introduced in 1947
[2]. Later, the Hosoya index, presented in 1971, emerged as
another infuential topological measure—see [9] for an in-
depth analysis. Building upon these early contributions, the
Zagreb indices (1972) and the R index were subsequently
formulated, greatly expanding the methodological frame-
work for modeling molecular structures and their physi-
cochemical properties [3, 10].
Consider a molecular graph G with vertex set V(G) and
edge set E(G). Te degree of a vertex v, written deg(v), is the
count of edges incident to v. Table 1 compiles the principal
degree-based topological indices that are widely investigated
in the literature and applied in the present analysis. Te
indices listed were selected in light of the smoothness results
reported by Kumar and Das [10], enabling a meaningful,
head-to-head comparison with the newly proposed Zagreb
Eta indices discussed later in Section 5.
All index defnitions follow standard formulations as
reported in references [3, 4, 11–25]. Tese equations are
widely accepted in the literature and are included here for
comparative and methodological completeness.
3. QSPR Modeling of Benzenes Using Zagreb
Eta Indices
Tis section investigates the strong statistical relationships
(r > 0.95) between the newly formulated Zagreb Eta indices
and major physicochemical attributes of benzene de-
rivatives, such as BP, Pi-ele, MW, PO, MV, and MR. Te
developed mathematical formulations quantitatively express
how structural variations infuence these properties in
benzenoid compounds. Recent works [5, 9, 25–32] provide
empirical evidence supporting the reliability of such cor-
relations. Table 2 lists the calculated Zagreb Eta indices for
a representative subset of benzene derivatives.
Figure 1 represents the 2D chemical structures of the
benzene derivatives analyzed in this study. Tese structures
were redrawn by the author using ChemDraw Ultra 12.0
software based on data obtained from the PubChem data-
base (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/).
Table 3 displays the physical-chemical properties of se-
lected benzene derivatives. Te data were derived from pre-
viously published experimental studies, particularly from
Nikoli´c et al., Hayat et al., and Malik et al., as cited in ref-
erences [26–28, 30]. Tis citation approach is intended to
enhance the reproducibility and traceability of the presented
data. Furthermore, the structure of our data citation is in-
spired by the data sourcing approach of Shanmukha et al. [6].
Te physicochemical parameters presented in Table 3 are
accompanied by their respective units. Specifcally, BP refers
to boiling point (°C), Pi-ele represents π-electron energy
(eV), MW denotes molecular weight (g/mol), PO indicates
polarizability (10−24 cm3), MV stands for molar volume
(cm3/mol), and MR represents molar refractivity (cm3/mol).
Tese units have been explicitly stated to improve the in-
terpretability and reproducibility of the presented data.
Table 4 summarizes the Pearson correlation coefcients
between the physicochemical parameters and the Zagreb Eta
indices of the analyzed benzenoid compounds.
Table 4 indicates that the correlation coefcients between
the three newly formulated Zagreb Eta indices and the
physicochemical characteristics of benzenoid compounds
are greater than 0.9299. Notably, for the third Zagreb Eta
index, the associations with MW, PO, and MR are nearly
perfect, with correlation values approaching unity. Tese
fndings represent the strongest relationships obtained in the
current investigation. Hence, it can be concluded that the
fundamental validation requirement for a newly proposed
topological index, as defned in this study, has been satis-
factorily met. Te subsequent fgures illustrate the linear

exhibit the highest correlation with the Zagreb Eta indices.

5. Theoretical Foundations of Zagreb
Eta Smoothness
Te conceptual foundation of the Eta degree and its
derivatives—the Zagreb Eta indices—refects a novel ad-
vancement in degree-based topological modeling. Tese
indices successfully incorporate molecular branching and
local connectivity features, which are critical for repre-
senting the structural complexity of benzenoid compounds.
Te strong correlations identifed between the Zagreb
Eta indices and molecular properties—including BP, Pi-ele,
enthalpy, and PO—are chemically meaningful. Tis re-
lationship arises from the planar aromatic framework of
benzenoid compounds, which supports a consistent topo-
logical interpretation of degree-based connectivity patterns.

Furtula et al. [5] to quantify the stability of molecular de-
scriptors. Recent studies [31, 32] extended this framework to
evaluate the SS of eigenvalue-based indices and to investigate
the continuity of graph energy in chemical structures. Te
algorithm outlined in [5] was employed in the present
analysis to compute SS and Abr for the Zagreb Eta indices
across diferent classes of graphs. Following the procedure of
Kumar and Das [4], the analysis was conducted for tree
graphs containing four to ten vertices, allowing comparison

Te SS and Abr values of the Zagreb Eta indices were
computed using the same algorithm for tree graphs con-
taining four to nine vertices, and the results are summarized
in Table 13.
For a topological index to be considered efective, it
should exhibit high SS and simultaneously maintain low Abr
values. When analyzing tree graphs with nine vertices, the
comparative results—contrasting Table 8 of this study with
Table 1 in reference [10] and Table 3 in reference [5]—reveal
that the Zagreb Eta indices achieve lower SS and Abr values
than all other degree-based descriptors. Tis indicates that
the proposed indices possess superior smoothness charac-
teristics, refecting stable behavior across variations in
molecular structure.
7. Limitations and Future Directions
Although the developed models exhibit strong correlations
between the Zagreb Eta indices and several physicochemical
characteristics of benzene derivatives, certain methodolog-
ical limitations should be acknowledged. First, the dataset
used in this study includes a relatively small number of
compounds, which may limit the extent to which the results
can be generalized to broader molecular families. Second,
the physicochemical parameters were collected from sec-
ondary sources such as published literature and chemical
databases; thus, inconsistencies due to variations in exper-
imental procedures or measurement conditions cannot be
completely ruled out.
Future work could involve expanding the dataset to
include more diverse classes of aromatic and nonaromatic
compounds, as well as exploring the applicability of alter-
native or hybrid topological indices. Additionally, in-
tegrating machine learning algorithms could enhance the
predictive power and robustness of the QSPR models.
8. Conclusion
In this research, the newly formulated Zagreb Eta indices
were employed to describe the relationships between mo-
lecular structure and physicochemical properties across a set
of benzene derivatives. Te statistical evaluation revealed
strong linear associations—exceeding 0.995 in several
cases—between the proposed indices and parameters such as
Pi-ele, MW, PO, and MR.
Tese results confrm the efectiveness of the Zagreb Eta
indices as degree-based topological descriptors in QSPR
modeling. Te indices show promising potential for broader
applications in cheminformatics, environmental chemistry,
and molecular design tasks.
